key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to call tools for the wrong reason, following superficial prompt cues instead of true task need.
engineering_relevance: For robust agent systems, tool-use policies should be trained and evaluated for causal necessity, not just success rate, because shortcut behaviors can silently degrade reliability.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue–tool correlations during training.
Ran counterfactual tests where cues appeared but the associated tools were not actually needed.
Added a dense, decision-level reward from an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was necessary.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared mainly after the agent had already learned the target tool reliably.
watch_item: The mitigation depends on an LLM judge to assess tool necessity, so reward quality and judge bias could affect robustness in real deployments.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
